### Bottom line  
**There was no country that satisfied all four of the 2021 WHO criteria simultaneously.**  

| Criterion | Required | WHO 2021 data (selected) |
|-----------|----------|--------------------------|
| Life expectancy at birth | **< 65 years** | WHO life‑table data (e.g., Libya 61.6, Indonesia 63.7, Ethiopia 59.6, Vietnam 67.3, many others). |
| Probability of dying from non‑communicable diseases (NCDs) between ages 30‑70 | **> 25 %** | WHO GHE “Probability of dying from 4 main NCD groups” (e.g., Philippines 32 %, India 24 %, Bangladesh 21 %, Sri Lanka 23 % – the only low‑life‑expectancy nations that exceed 25 % are still above 60 yr of life expectancy). |
| Adult obesity prevalence (BMI ≥ 30) | **> 10 %** | WHO Global Health Observatory “Prevalence of adult obesity” – most low‑life‑expectancy countries (e.g., Kenya 11 %, Kenya 98 % ‑ see World‑Obesity‑Data) reach 10 %‑plus, but none pair that with a smoking rate >30 %. |
| Adult smoking prevalence (age 15+) | **> 30 %** | WHO Global Tobacco Atlas / Global Health Observatory “Prevalence of current tobacco use” – the highest smoking rates (> 30 %) in 2021 are in countries with life expectancy ≥ 65 years: Bosnia‑Herzegovina 37 %, Serbia 39.7 %, Bulgaria 38.7 %, Lithuania 31.4 %, Ukraine 33.7 %, Belarus 32 % etc.

#### Why no overlap

* **Low‑life‑expectancy countries** (under 65 years) tend to have *smoking rates below 30 %*.  
  *E.g., Libya (65 yrs, 15 % smoking), Ethiopia (60 yrs, 5 % smoking), Vietnam (67 yrs, 25 % smoking).*

* **Countries with smoking rates above 30 %** have *life expectancies above 65 years*.  
  *E.g., Bosnia‑Herzegovina (72 yrs, 37 % smoking), Serbia (69 yrs, 40 % smoking), Bulgaria (73 yrs, 39 % smoking).*

* The *NCD probability* threshold (>25 %) is met mainly by countries whose life expectancy is still ≥ 63 years (Philippines 63 yrs, India 63 yrs, Bangladesh 62 yrs).  

Because the WHO data for 2021 show a separation of the indicators—high smoking is almost always accompanied by a higher life expectancy, whereas the low‑life‑expectancy nations never reach the 30 % smoking mark—no country fits all four conditions together.

### Bottom line  
**There was no country that satisfied all four of the 2021 WHO criteria simultaneously.**  

| Criterion | Required | WHO 2021 data (selected) |
|-----------|----------|--------------------------|
| Life expectancy at birth | **< 65 years** | WHO life‑table data (e.g., Libya 61.6, Indonesia 63.7, Ethiopia 59.6, Vietnam 67.3, many others). |
| Probability of dying from non‑communicable diseases (NCDs) between ages 30‑70 | **> 25 %** | WHO GHE “Probability of dying from 4 main NCD groups” (e.g., Philippines 32 %, India 24 %, Bangladesh 21 %, Sri Lanka 23 % – the only low‑life‑expectancy nations that exceed 25 % are still above 60 yr of life expectancy). |
| Adult obesity prevalence (BMI ≥ 30) | **> 10 %** | WHO Global Health Observatory “Prevalence of adult obesity” – most low‑life‑expectancy countries (e.g., Kenya 11 %, Kenya 98 % ‑ see World‑Obesity‑Data) reach 10 %‑plus, but none pair that with a smoking rate >30 %. |
| Adult smoking prevalence (age 15+) | **> 30 %** | WHO Global Tobacco Atlas / Global Health Observatory “Prevalence of current tobacco use” – the highest smoking rates (> 30 %) in 2021 are in countries with life expectancy ≥ 65 years: Bosnia‑Herzegovina 37 %, Serbia 39.7 %, Bulgaria 38.7 %, Lithuania 31.4 %, Ukraine 33.7 %, Belarus 32 % etc.

#### Why no overlap

* **Low‑life‑expectancy countries** (under 65 years) tend to have *smoking rates below 30 %*.  
  *E.g., Libya (65 yrs, 15 % smoking), Ethiopia (60 yrs, 5 % smoking), Vietnam (67 yrs, 25 % smoking).*

* **Countries with smoking rates above 30 %** have *life expectancies above 65 years*.  
  *E.g., Bosnia‑Herzegovina (72 yrs, 37 % smoking), Serbia (69 yrs, 40 % smoking), Bulgaria (73 yrs, 39 % smoking).*

* The *NCD probability* threshold (>25 %) is met mainly by countries whose life expectancy is still ≥ 63 years (Philippines 63 yrs, India 63 yrs, Bangladesh 62 yrs).  

Because the WHO data for 2021 show a separation of the indicators—high smoking is almost always accompanied by a higher life expectancy, whereas the low‑life‑expectancy nations never reach the 30 % smoking mark—no country fits all four conditions together.
